unit: one axle shaft seal (differential or transaxle output seal) at one side, fitted, with the gear oil or transmission fluid top-up the job requires. Not included: the wheel or axle bearing, the axle shaft itself, a full fluid drain and refill service, the seal on the other side, the pinion seal
held_reason: First attempt, 2026-11-20. Only the truck class has a labor range, and both ends are a parts seller's approximate install time (1 hour and 4 hours), not a book time. Economy, midsize and luxury have no labor range: every maker bulletin found either replaces the axle shaft or a second seal along with the seal, or prints the time with no unit. No class has an aftermarket price from a page that says new, and economy, midsize and luxury have no confirmed list price either. Needs: a seal-only time with a unit for a front-wheel-drive car, an all-wheel-drive crossover and a luxury-make car, a retailer page that says new for each class, and a dealer catalog page that ties the seal part number to the example vehicle.

finding: New job, so there is no live range to judge, and this file is not ready to show a range. Built totals use parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks). Only the truck class can be partly built: on a 2010 Ford F-150 with the 9.75-inch rear axle the labor is 1 to 4 hours ($120-$640), and with the seal at Ford's list price of $58.40 the total is about $178-$698; no low total with an aftermarket seal is given because none of the retailer pages ($15.68, $19.79, $25.89) says the seal is new. The seal is a small part of the bill in every class seen ($10-$60), so the total is almost all labor and the labor time is what matters. How solid the labor times are: weak. The truck range is two parts sellers' approximate install times for the same axle, and a spread of 1 to 4 hours is too wide to judge a quote with. Economy, midsize and luxury have no usable time. The maker bulletins found do not print a seal-only time: GM allows 0.7 hr on a Chevrolet Equinox to replace the left front drive shaft and its seal together; Mazda allows 1.5 hours on a CX-9 AWD for the right-side transfer seal with its dust seal and deflector; Nissan prints 1.0 to 2.2 for the right front axle seal on its AWD models with no unit; GM allows 1.6 hours on 2019-2020 Silverado front axles for a stub shaft, seal and O-ring; Tesla prints 1.02 with no unit for a Model 3 rear output seal. Ford, FCA, Subaru and Honda bulletins loaded either covered a different part or printed no time. Taken together the cross-checks point to roughly 0.7 to 2.2 hours per seal on cars and crossovers, which at $120-$160/hr would be about $85-$350 of labor, but that is a reading of cross-checks, not a sourced range. Parts: no list price could be tied to the 2015 Corolla or the BMW 328i (F30) seal on the pages loaded. Against the outside estimates: the partial truck total ($178-$698) brackets RepairPal's national figure ($363-$509), YourMechanic's F-150 rear-seal rows ($176-$318) and ConsumerAffairs' single F-150 figure ($287); RepairPal assumes $311-$457 of labor, which at $120-$160/hr is roughly 1.9 to 3.8 hours.
extras: A quote often adds a leak diagnosis or inspection fee, a full gear oil or transmission fluid drain and refill in place of a top-up, a new axle nut, circlip or other one-time-use fasteners, the wheel or axle bearing if it is worn, an axle shaft or CV axle if the sealing surface is grooved, the seal on the other side, brake shoes or pads if gear oil has soaked them, a differential cover gasket or sealant on axles where the cover comes off to release the shafts, shop supplies and sales tax.
